item.title: Remember Who You Are — Greater Is He Who Is in You
item.description:
Read: Scripture 1 John 4:4–18 NIV
Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 56 NIV

Fear has a way of making things feel larger than they really are. A thought can become overwhelming, a worry can grow until it seems to fill the whole room, and something uncertain can begin to feel more powerful than everything we know to be true. But the Bible reminds us of something simple and important: what frightens us is not greater than the God who is with us.

item.title: Building a Publishing System That Helps Me Think
item.description:
Over the last few weeks I’ve been writing more.

That has created a slightly unexpected problem.

Writing the article itself was never really the whole problem. I needed somewhere for ideas to start, somewhere they could develop, somewhere finished thinking could live, and a sensible way of sharing it.

For a while those things were all getting mixed together.

I had notes in Obsidian. Drafts developed through conversations. Articles on LinkedIn. Older posts elsewhere. Ideas that were clearly related to one another but were effectively trapped inside individual documents.

item.title: Be Strong and Courageous
item.description:
Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV

Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.

Joshua was facing something enormous. Moses had died, and after years of watching Moses lead Israel, Joshua was now responsible for leading the people into the land God had promised them. Thousands of people were looking to him, there were enemies ahead, and Joshua couldn’t possibly know exactly what was going to happen.

item.title: Borrowing Horizons
item.description:
My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.

“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”

Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.

What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.

item.title: From Coding Agents to Loop Engineering: Building Engineering Memory for AI
item.description: Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow becomes more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but fundamentally it is still a pipeline.

item.title: If God Knows, Why Pray?
item.description:
After hours · a continuing series

Late Night Questions

My wife is a midwife, and some of the more difficult theological and ethical questions in our house have a habit of arriving after a late shift, usually when we're both tired and neither of us is expecting a theological discussion.

This series is an attempt to keep track of those questions: not necessarily to find a neat answer, but to look at Scripture, draw on writers who have helped me think, and work out what I actually believe and why.

item.title: Remember Who You Are — Do Not Be Afraid
item.description:
Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV
Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 27 NIV

There are many things that can make us afraid. Sometimes we know exactly what we are frightened of; sometimes we simply feel afraid and cannot explain why. Our thoughts can become confused, things that once seemed familiar can feel uncertain, and we may wonder what is happening or what will happen next.

But there is something that has not changed: God is with you. He has not moved away from you, he has not forgotten you, and he has not stopped loving you. Again and again in the Bible, God tells his people, “Do not be afraid.” He does not say this because there is never anything frightening in life, but because we do not face those things alone.

item.title: Starting Again — Family Devotions
item.description:
There are some things we know are important and yet still struggle to do consistently.

Reading the Bible has, at different points in my life, been one of those things. Family devotions have been another. I have ADHD, and consistency and discipline are things I’ve always struggled with. I can become deeply absorbed in something, build a routine around it and then, somehow, find that routine has disappeared. There have been periods when I’ve read Scripture regularly and periods when I’ve let it drift. In recent years the same has happened with sitting down regularly as a family to read the Bible and pray together.

item.title: When Things Change
item.description:
Read: Scripture Psalm 46:1–7 NIV

Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.

Change can be difficult. Sometimes it is not even the change itself that is hardest, but the uncertainty that comes with it. We might know how yesterday worked, but suddenly we are not quite sure what tomorrow will look like.

That can happen when we start somewhere new, perhaps a new school, class or group. We need to learn where we fit, who people are and how things work. But change can happen in familiar places too. Someone we know might begin behaving differently towards us. A friendship might feel different. Something that once seemed easy can suddenly become confusing, and we can find ourselves wondering what we are supposed to do next.

item.title: When Trust Becomes the Constraint
item.description:
One of the more difficult problems I keep coming back to with AI-assisted software modernisation isn’t really a technology problem. It’s trust.

We have all seen an LLM confidently make something up, merge two facts that happened to look similar, or produce an explanation that sounds entirely reasonable until someone who really understands the domain reads it. Once you have seen that happen a few times, it changes how you approach the capability, and that matters when we start asking AI to help modernise software.

item.title: Human in the loop isn’t the same as human judgement
item.description:
“Human in the loop” has become one of the standard answers to concerns about AI. We do not entirely trust the model, so we put a person somewhere in the process to validate what it has done. On the surface that sounds sensible, and sometimes it absolutely is.

But I think it exposes a much older problem in the way we design controls.

I’ve spent a lot of time working with security and compliance teams, and more recently with OT security teams where getting controls wrong can affect physical assets and operations as well as systems and data. I’ve seen similar patterns in higher education and charities, where safeguarding, accountability and practicality have to coexist across both physical and digital boundaries.

item.title: Dependencies are a design choice
item.description:
I’ve been building a wall of shelves in my office.

Like most DIY jobs, it started with a fairly simple picture in my head and rapidly became a network of dependencies. I couldn’t cut a shelf accurately until the uprights were fixed. I couldn’t fix the next section until I knew how the previous one actually sat against a wall that was considerably less straight than it looked. Some pieces could be measured once and reproduced. Others genuinely had to wait until something else was complete.

item.title: Lowering the Cost of Curiosity
item.description:
I have been doing a lot of experimentation with local models recently, as have many of my colleagues. There is also a growing anticipation around the next generation of developer workstations and AI-focused boxes: machines capable of running increasingly useful models without sending every request to a SaaS platform.

It is easy to see this as another technology choice: local versus cloud, open model versus proprietary model, workstation versus API. I think the more interesting question for enterprises is economic.

item.title: What DevOps Taught Me About Managing ADHD, Attention and Flow
item.description:
I was chatting recently with someone else who has ADHD about how I manage notes, tasks and to-dos. What surprised me was that the useful bit wasn’t really the tools. It was the process I’d gone through to get there.

I was diagnosed with ADHD relatively recently, and that gave me a useful lens for understanding why some of my productivity systems had worked for a while and then gradually collapsed under their own weight. I don’t want to dwell on the diagnosis itself here. What mattered was the reframing.

item.title: Running Backstage in Dev Container
item.description:
Okay so I’ve been wanting to make the process of getting up and running with backstage simpler. The aim is to setup a full environment with containers for

  • IAM
  • Documentation Generation
  • Cloud Cost Extraction
  • Terraform Deployment / Destruction
  • Model to track resources deployed by via terraform

Other features will include:

  • Helm chart for full deployment
  • CI pipeline for deployment to kubernetes
  • Set of project templates for my own use
    • Hugo Site
    • dotnet API
    • node API
    • golang API
    • Python API
    • orgmode project starter
    • Python GenAI project, including RAG

I’m really looking to meld together the infrastructure and deployment side of things.

item.title: Automating Hugo Site Deployment with GitHub Actions and Private Repositories
item.description:
I’ve always been a proponent of DevOps, and my recent experiments with Hugo have led me to automate the deployment of my site. This post details how I set up an automatic deployment process for my Hugo site using GitHub Actions while keeping my drafts and content private until I’m ready to share them.

Keeping a Private Repository for Hugo Site Definition
#

I have a private repository for my Hugo site definition to keep my draft posts and other content secure until they’re ready for the public. The objective was straightforward: whenever I commit changes to the main branch, Hugo runs, and the result is committed to another repository, specifically my GitHub Pages repo.

item.title: I love it when a plan comes together
item.description: So I thought these posts would happen more regularly; it’s just been intense getting to know so many people. Bringing together three teams distributed across our campuses has been a great deal of fun. Each is unique, with its distinct strengths and culture. Today I shared our strategy for IT across the group. While I get nervous speaking in front of people, I love these moments. It’s the big reveal of the analysis and work that has been amassed over the last 6 months. While I’m not going to share the whole presentation, I will run through the top-level framework and a couple of the guiding principles.

item.title: An Entertaining Start
item.description: So at the beginning of the month I began a new adventure as an employee for the first time in 7 years, starting as the new Group Director for IT with Eastern Colleges Group. I really am excited about this role, there is so much to get to grips with, so many areas in which IT directly contributes to the eduction delivered by the colleges. I’ll be posting sporadically (if I ever get this blog published) with how the role is going and the challeges that we face in ensuring that the systems keep working.

item.title: Getting Running With Hugo
item.description:
Choosing the Right Environment for Hugo Development: My Journey to Containers
#

When it comes to setting up a development environment for Hugo, there are numerous options available. My journey in selecting the most suitable one was guided by a desire for efficiency and minimal impact on my primary workstation. Here, I share my experience and rationale behind choosing containers over other methods.

item.title: Getting Started
item.description:
So I’ve started building a new site here as a set of github pages. This has mainly involved playing with couple of site generators, and seeing how I get on with them.

My motivation in this is pretty simple I need to get better at blogging. The tooling I use is a big contributing factor to that. To that end I’ve been trying out a number of platforms and here are the results.

item.title: The Unicorn Project
item.description: I’ve had the privilege to get early access to The Unicorn Project by Gene Kim. Set within Parts Unlimited a large manufacturing and retail organisation that is struggling to come to terms with software as a first class citizen. Yes for those of you who have read The Phoenix Project this story is set in the same organisation and you see many of the same characters and events that occurred. In fact this tale follows another character within the narrative that was only briefly introduced before, namely a developer.

item.title: An Example of Flow
item.description: I’ve been reading The Goal as well as The Phoenix Project. Whilst there are many important principals in these novels and I highly recommend them. I wanted to highlight one in particular. The danger of too much Inventory or unfinished work. Recently I was working on an Agile project. This team conformed to the scrum framework zealously, the application architecture was solid, the team were beyond excellent, we had fantastic and driven product owner. Yet despite all of this we consistently missed our sprint goal. Each retrospective we looked at the process adjusted and tried again. We reduced sprint lengths reduced the number of stories in a sprint, inflated our estimates for the stories, and quite a number of other adjustments, nothing seemed to resolve the issue. We were confounded nothing seemed to resolve what was happening. Finally Matt the Scrum Master suggest one last thing.
